has_highs <- requireNamespace("highs", quietly = TRUE)

```{r setup}
library(multimod)
mod <- example_models$energyRt$multimod
mod
```

## The flexibility-performance tradeoff

Framework models such as energyRt are written to cover many cases: one
generic set of equations covers technologies, storage, trade, emissions and
more, and every parameter is indexed over every dimension it may vary by
(technology, commodity, region, year, timeslice). A given scenario uses only
part of that:

- a single-region model has no interregional trade,
- most technologies have the same efficiency in every timeslice,
- features the scenario does not use leave sets and mappings empty, and the
  equations that depend on them generate no constraints.

This generality has a cost at model-build time and in the solver: data that
is repeated across a dimension inflates the data files and the coefficient
count, and equations with empty domains are still processed. multimod offers
two complementary transformations that remove this redundancy without changing
the optimum, as the appendix verifies:

1. **Folding** removes a dimension from a parameter when the values are
   constant across it (data redundancy).
2. **Trimming** marks sets, parameters, mappings, variables and equations that
   have no data or no instances, so code generators skip them (structural
   redundancy).

Both are reversible, and both are honored by the MathProg, JuMP, Pyomo and
LaTeX writers and by the matrix route.

## Folding

### The idea

Consider a 5-dimensional parameter whose values do not depend on the timeslice:

```
pTechCinp2use[E01, ELC, R1, 2025, s1] = 0.95
pTechCinp2use[E01, ELC, R1, 2025, s2] = 0.95
...
```

Folding drops the `timeslice` dimension and keeps one row per remaining index
combination. Equations that reference the parameter are rewritten to omit the
folded index:

```
# before
vTechInp[t,c,r,y,s] >= pTechCinp2use[t,c,r,y,s] * vTechAct[t,r,y,s]
# after
vTechInp[t,c,r,y,s] >= pTechCinp2use[t,c,r,y]   * vTechAct[t,r,y,s]
```

### Diagnose redundancy

`analyze_parameter_redundancy()` reports, per parameter, how many rows carry a
repeated value. High redundancy marks a folding candidate.

```{r redundancy}
red <- analyze_parameter_redundancy(mod, verbose = FALSE)
red <- red[order(-red$orig_redundancy_pct), ]
head(red[, c("param_name", "dims", "orig_rows", "orig_unique",
             "orig_redundancy_pct")], 8)
```

### Build a fold specification

`create_fold_spec()` takes `fold_dims`, a named list: one entry per dimension to
fold, whose value names the *validation mappings* to check against. For an
energyRt model the technology parameters are validated against
`mTechTimeslice` and the commodity parameters against `mCommTimeslice`:

```{r fold-spec}
fold_spec <- create_fold_spec(
  mod,
  fold_dims = list(
    timeslice = list(tech = "mTechTimeslice", comm = "mCommTimeslice")
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)
fold_spec[, c("param_name", "validation_mapping", "can_fold", "unproven")]
```

The result is a data frame with one row per parameter that carries the
dimension. `can_fold` is `TRUE` when the values are constant across the
dimension in every group formed by the other indices. `unproven` flags
parameters that failed only because no validation mapping was found for their
entity type; supplying one (for example `sup = "mSupTimeslice"`) would let them
be checked.

The validation mapping matters because a parameter may be constant across the
timeslice *in the data* only because the scenario never varied it. The mapping
states which entities may vary by that dimension, so folding stays consistent
with the model structure, not only with one dataset. A value of
`c("mStorageComm", "mCommTimeslice")` chains two mappings when the entity is
linked to the dimension indirectly.

Several dimensions can be folded in one specification; they are applied in the
order given, each on the result of the previous one:

```{r fold-spec-multi, eval = FALSE}
create_fold_spec(
  mod,
  fold_dims = list(
    timeslice = list(tech = "mTechTimeslice", comm = "mCommTimeslice"),
    region    = list(comm = "mCommRegion")
  )
)
```

### Apply the fold

```{r fold}
mod_folded <- fold_model(mod, fold_spec = fold_spec, verbose = FALSE)
is_folded(mod)
is_folded(mod_folded)
```

`fold_model()` collapses the data of every parameter with `can_fold = TRUE`,
rewrites each equation that references one of them, and records what it did
in `model$misc$fold_summary`. `get_fold_summary()` reads that record:

```{r fold-summary}
get_fold_summary(mod_folded, format = "data.frame")[
  , c("parameter", "removed_dims", "original_rows", "folded_rows", "compression")]
```

With `format = "text"` the same information is printed as a report;
`format = "list"` returns it as nested lists.

### Inspect a folded parameter

`is_folded()` also works on a single parameter, and `get_active_dims()` returns
the dimensions in force after folding; the declaration stays in `$dims`.

```{r active-dims}
p <- mod_folded$parameters$pTechCinp2use
is_folded(p)
p$dims              # as declared
get_active_dims(p)  # in force after folding

# parameters the fold did not touch keep their declaration
is_folded(mod_folded$parameters$pTechInvcost)
```

The fold metadata lives in `p$misc$fold_info`:

```{r fold-info}
p$misc$fold_info[c("original_dims", "removed_dims", "original_rows",
                   "folded_rows", "compression_ratio")]
```

### Unfold

`unfold_model()` restores the original data and dimensions of every folded
parameter:

```{r unfold}
mod_unfolded <- unfold_model(mod_folded, verbose = FALSE)
nrow(mod_unfolded$parameters$pTechCinp2use$data)
nrow(mod$parameters$pTechCinp2use$data)
```

### Aliases and repeated dimensions

A parameter can be declared with one dimension name while its data uses an
alias column (`comm` declared, `acomm` in the data), or a dimension can appear
twice in different roles (`{region, region}` stored as `src`, `dst`). Folding
resolves the first through `model$aliases` and keeps every data column other
than the folded one for the second, so both cases fold without special
handling.

## Trimming

### The idea

A scenario rarely exercises every feature of a framework model. Elements that
end up without data or without instances are:

- **empty sets and mappings** (no storage technologies, no trade routes),
- **empty parameters**,
- **variables** indexed by an empty set,
- **equations** whose domain is empty, or that only reference trimmed
  variables.

Trimming marks these with `$trimmed = TRUE`. Nothing is deleted; code
generators and `write_latex()` check the flag and skip (or annotate) the
element.

### Four phases

```
1. mark sets, parameters and mappings with no data
2. mark variables whose domain is empty
3. mark equations with an empty domain, or with only trimmed variables
4. untrim anything a non-trimmed equation still uses
```

Phase 4 is what keeps trimming conservative: an element is only trimmed when
no surviving equation needs it.

### Apply the trim

Folding comes first: it can empty a parameter that trimming then removes.

```{r trim}
mod_trimmed <- trim_model(mod_folded, verbose = FALSE)
is_trimmed(mod)
is_trimmed(mod_trimmed)
get_trim_summary(mod_trimmed, format = "data.frame")
```

The example scenario uses a small share of the energyRt equations, so most of
them trim away. As with folding, `format = "text"` prints a report and
`format = "list"` returns nested lists. `is_trimmed()` works on individual
elements too:

```{r trim-elements}
is_trimmed(mod_trimmed$equations$eqTechCap)
is_trimmed(mod_trimmed$equations$eqTechInpTot)
head(get_trim_summary(mod_trimmed, format = "list")$equations$names)
```

### Untrim

`untrim_model()` clears the flags, on all element types by default or on the
ones named in `elements`:

```{r untrim}
mod_back <- untrim_model(mod_trimmed)
is_trimmed(mod_back)
```

## Folding versus trimming

| | Folding | Trimming |
|---|---|---|
| Targets | data redundancy | structural redundancy |
| Mechanism | collapses a constant dimension | flags unused elements |
| Reduces | parameter rows, coefficient count | sets, parameters, variables, equations emitted |
| Needs | a fold specification (validation mappings) | nothing; driven by the data |
| Reversed by | `unfold_model()` | `untrim_model()` |

**Folding** applies when parameters are constant across a dimension the
scenario does not need (timeslice is the usual case), when data files or
solver memory are the bottleneck, or when a model written for many regions or
years is run with one.

**Trimming** applies when the scenario leaves optional features unused, when
empty sets or parameters exist, or when many equations generate no
constraints.

**Both** suit framework models, folding first and trimming second. The
objective of a transformed model is worth comparing with the original's before
relying on it (see the appendix).

Folding and trimming change what the generated model *contains*; they do not
change what it *means*. A dimension that varies in the data is not foldable
(`create_fold_spec()` refuses it, although a hand-edited specification can
override that), and an untrimmed copy remains useful when the complete
structure is wanted for documentation or comparison.

## Writing transformed models

The writers honor the flags. `write_gmpl()`, `write_jump()` and
`write_pyomo()` use the folded dimensions by default and skip trimmed
elements; `write_latex()` chooses `model_view = "reduced"` for a folded or
trimmed model and annotates the removed elements in `model_view = "full"`.
`model_to_lp()` and `solve_highs()` assemble the matrix from the active
dimensions directly.

```{r write, eval = FALSE}
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "trimmed")
save_model(mod_trimmed, dir, format = "ipc")
write_gmpl(mod_trimmed, model_dir = dir)
write_jump(mod_trimmed, model_dir = dir)
write_latex(mod_trimmed, file = file.path(dir, "model.tex"), model_view = "full")
```

A fold specification is an ordinary data frame; saved with `saveRDS()`, it
reproduces the transformation on another scenario of the same model.

## Limitations

- Folding is all-or-nothing per parameter: either every group is constant
  across the dimension or the parameter is left alone.
- Folding needs validation mappings that reflect the model's structure; for a
  model other than energyRt, the specification names the mappings that link
  each entity to the dimension.
- Folding loads the parameter data into memory while it runs.
- Trimming only flags elements; the data stays on disk and in the object.
- Trimming is conservative by design: it never removes an element a surviving
  equation references, so unused variables inside non-empty equations are kept.

## Appendix: the objective is unchanged

The transformed models solve to the same objective as the original. The check
below uses the matrix route with the 'highs' package.

```{r verify, eval = has_highs}
r0 <- solve_highs(mod, attach = FALSE)
r1 <- solve_highs(mod_folded, attach = FALSE)
r2 <- solve_highs(mod_trimmed, attach = FALSE)
c(original = r0$objective, folded = r1$objective, trimmed = r2$objective)
all.equal(r0$objective, r1$objective)
all.equal(r0$objective, r2$objective)
```
